title: We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose
author: Nick McMillan
content:
After President Donald Trump’s “emergency” tariffs were overturned by the
Supreme Court in February 2026, the government began processing billions in
refunds to importers, including many recognizable public companies.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting
roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for. ProPublica
requested the information, but U.S. Customs and Border Protection denied our
requests. (We’re appealing.)

So our reporters found another way: analyzing the financial disclosures of
thousands of publicly traded companies.

Today, ProPublica published [“Cash Back,” a database of figures on refunds for
tariffs](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-tariff-refund-ieepa/) paid
under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The database includes
343 public companies for which we found mentions of refunds, amounting to more
than $28 billion recovered or expected.

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261021-Celi_Tariff-Refund-
Tracker-3x2_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **See How
Much Companies Are Getting in Tariff Refunds**
](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-tariff-refund-ieepa/)

At least nine companies have disclosed that they are using their refunds not
to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the
tariff costs through higher prices, [but to give
bonuses](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-tariff-refunds-corporate-
bonuses), according to a ProPublica analysis published earlier this week.

Recognizable businesses include the tool company Stanley Black & Decker and
the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls, and the golf
equipment brand Titleist.

Many other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money.

ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded
companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None
of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said
they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their
refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such
information.

[Explore the Cash Back database here.](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-
tariff-refund-ieepa/)

### What’s included in the database?

The [Supreme Court
ruled](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/25pdf/24-1287_4gcj.pdf) on Feb.
20, 2026, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act doesn’t
authorize the president to impose tariffs. The U.S. Court of International
Trade ordered U.S. Customs and Border Protection to refund the duties it had
collected.

This tracker covers refunds on those tariffs disclosed by publicly traded
companies. Public companies must disclose events that affect their finances,
such as tariff payments and refunds, on earnings calls and in regular reports
filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We collected information
from these public sources through Oct. 7, 2026.

Before publishing, we contacted all companies shown here to check the accuracy
of the numbers we had found.

We grouped companies by industry using a combination of [designations from
Morningstar](https://www.morningstar.com/sectors).

### How did we determine refund amounts?

ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls using key
phrases to isolate companies that mentioned tariff refunds. For each company,
we created a document that included the extracted text around each phrase. For
SEC filings, that included parsed Extensible Business Reporting Language when
available.

We then used an open-weight artificial intelligence model for a first pass at
identifying refund amounts. ProPublica reporters reviewed each company by hand
to make sure our database is accurate and contacted all companies to confirm
the amounts.

Companies normally record tariff refunds in their financial statements under
two accounting models:

  * Gain contingency: when the refund has been received or recovery is essentially certain.
  * Loss recovery: when the refund is probable and can be reasonably estimated.

To determine a company’s recovered refund, we added up the amounts it recorded
that were essentially certain or probable (sometimes known as “receivable”),
plus the amounts it disclosed as having been received.

The government is required to pay interest on tariff amounts it is returning,
at rates [determined by the
IRS](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/22/2026-01175/quarterly-
irs-interest-rates-used-in-calculating-interest-on-overdue-accounts-and-
refunds-of-customs) on a quarterly basis. Companies disclosed that interest in
different ways. Some reported the refund and the interest separately, while
others reported a single amount that included both. When a company reported
them separately, we added the interest to the refund to capture the full
amount of money that a company was receiving from the government.

Some companies reported only their net refund instead of the full amount
received. For example, a company might report only what was left of the tariff
refund after reinvesting into its business or after passing part of the refund
onto customers. In these cases, we reported the net amount. When companies
reported a range, we used the lower end. In both cases, we noted that
information on the company page.

The specific security filings reviewed were: 8-K, 10-Q, 10-K, 8-K/A, 10-Q/A,
10-K/A, 6-K, 6-K/A, 20-F, 20-F/A, 40-F, 40-F/A and any associated exhibits.

### Can I get a refund?

Only importers or the authorized custom brokers who filed the entries can
submit a request for a refund. That means that even if companies passed tariff
costs on to customers through higher prices, the refund goes to the company,
and it is up to the company to determine how the money is used.

[UPS](https://www.ups.com/us/en/shipping/international-
shipping/tariffs/tariff-refunds) and [FedEx](https://ieepa-refunds.fedex.com/)
are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them. The
companies have set up online portals for customers to track their refunds.
Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on
behalf of businesses and individuals who paid them to ship products.

Other companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their
refund checks with their customers, though these companies’ customers are
generally other businesses. Trade experts say these business-to-business
vendors likely have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.

Some companies have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for
example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though
they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future
increases.  

### How do I report incorrect information?

If you see information that may be incorrect, please email
[tariffs@propublica.org](mailto:tariffs@propublica.org).

We will periodically update our database by pulling information from newer
filings, as well as correcting or adding new information when companies reach
out to us.

### Can I download the data?

Yes, you can [download the data here](https://github.com/propublica/cash-back-
tariff-data). We ask that you credit “ProPublica analysis of financial
disclosures” and link to [this tracker](https://projects.propublica.org/trump-
tariff-refund-ieepa/).

### Do you have information you can share about how a company is using tariff
refunds?

ProPublica’s investigative journalists are reporting on tariff refunds and
how, or if, companies are giving money back to consumers. You can reach [our
tip line](https://www.propublica.org/tips/) or contact us on Signal at
917-512-0201. Please be as specific, detailed and clear as you can.

The post [We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to
Disclose](https://www.propublica.org/article/tariff-refund-database-cash-back)
appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
